name: Sharpen a kitchen knife
blurb: The single highest-impact kitchen skill that is not cooking. A sharp knife is safer, faster and more pleasant, and whetstone sharpening takes about a week to learn properly.
gear: A combination whetstone, roughly 1000 and 3000 grit
A damp cloth to stop the stone sliding
steps: Soak the stone if it is a soaking type, and set it on a non-slip base.
Find the angle: most European knives want about 20 degrees per side, Japanese knives about 15. Colour the bevel with a marker to see exactly what you are removing.
Grind one side with even strokes, edge leading, covering the whole blade including the tip, until a burr forms along the entire opposite edge.
Flip and repeat until the burr forms on the first side.
Refine on the finer grit with lighter alternating strokes, then strop on cardboard or leather to remove the burr.
Test on paper, then a tomato. Learn to hone with the rod between sharpenings to keep the edge straight.
tips: Honing is not sharpening. A rod realigns an edge, a stone removes metal. Do both, at different frequencies.
Pull-through sharpeners tear the edge and shorten the life of a good knife.
Consistency of angle beats everything else. A slightly wrong but consistent angle is far better than a wandering correct one.
proof: A blunt knife you sharpened cleanly slices a ripe tomato under its own weight.
